(may use /). When a work has no entry, build-work-page.mjs emits its generic paragraph. Curated prose lives HERE, never only in generated site HTML — rebuilds must be safe.
9741: Abbo, abbot of Fleury, addressed this collection of canons to Hugh Capet and his son Robert about 995–996 — a mirror of royal duty and a defense of the monastic order, stitched from councils, the Theodosian code, and the fathers. The Latin is Migne's printing (PL 139, coll. 473A–508A), from the Corpus Corporum transcription; Migne's text descends from the early modern editions and prints fifty-two chapters, where the one complete manuscript carries forty-four. Parenthetical references in small type stand on Migne's page — editorial identifications inherited from the edition he reprinted or supplied by his shop, not Abbo's; the author's own citations run in the prose itself. Every gilt column mark is an address: migne.app/pl/139/473a resolves to the first.
7561: The Commonitorium — a title best rendered 'reminder' or 'memorandum' — was written on the island of Lérins about 434 by the monk Vincent, who signs himself Peregrinus, the Pilgrim. It is the classic Western statement of how the Church holds its faith across time: the catholic rule is what has been believed everywhere, always, and by all (quod ubique, quod semper, quod ab omnibus creditum est), and doctrine grows only as a body grows, developing without ever becoming something other than itself. Migne prints the surviving first book together with the recapitulation that is all that remains of the lost second (PL 50, coll. 637C–686B), from the Corpus Corporum transcription of Baluze's edition. This is not the first English of the Commonitorium — it has been translated before, notably by C. A. Heurtley in the Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers and by Rudolph Morris in the Fathers of the Church — and we make no claim otherwise. We render it afresh because a text this central to how the tradition understands itself belongs in migne.app's own voice, set beside its Latin column for column. The gilt marks carry Migne's numbering: migne.app/pl/50/637 resolves to the opening.
7383: This short exposition of the Magnificat — Mary's canticle from the first chapter of Luke — comes down without an author's name. Migne prints it among the appendix of works gathered under Augustine's name but not by him (PL 40, coll. 1137–1142), where much of the pseudo-Augustinian and anonymous material of the tradition was collected; the Latin here is the Corpus Corporum transcription of that printing. We render it as it stands, anonymous, letting the text speak for itself. The gilt column marks carry Migne's own numbering: migne.app/pl/40/1137 resolves to the opening.
